title: Allegory vs. Myth
english: We say that there are no perceptible things in the place. By interpreting these things, he does not err in calling a myth what God is said to have created and what Moses, the most faithful servant of God, wrote; rather, from the opposites which a myth formed in the belly offers up obscurely, he confirms these things in a dogmatic writing, showing them to be true.

It is worthy to remain unshaken in the belief that the words of the belly-myth were spoken through the Holy Spirit, having sworn to seem like the Scripture; but calling the messages sent through Moses by God 'myth' fluctuates the meaning, not remaining faithful to the literal sense of the letter.

But does he not allegorize the wells dug by Abraham and those around him, and after constructing such a chain of words, does he not refute their entire reality by shifting them into another sense, even though you will still see the wells appearing in places even now? Did he not turn the matters of Isaac and Rebekah into allegories, having said that the words about the ears and the clefts were golden, but having seized the whole hypothesis and applying it to the intelligible, he acted as a slanderer? Regarding Job, instead of marveling at his endurance, he praised the labors, spoke well of his excellence, accepted the faith, expressed the examples of his patient soul, and through this encouraged the new converts to virtue, arming the combatants with a cheerful and strong wisdom to strive bravely for piety; but leaving him, he rushed meteorically toward the names of the daughters, grinding them down crudely. As for how he puffed up the name of the Day and of Cassia, or even the horn of Amalthea, he does not even say such a thing; for he is a vessel of all kinds of overflow.

Writing about Lazarus, instead of glorifying the great work of Christ and thereby clearly proving that God is the one who, by authority, sent the dead man out of the tombs and, by the release of the word, gave life to the corruptible bodies, he says nothing for this reason, but through allegory leads the friend of the Lord, Lazarus, whom he did not love unsuitably through virtue, to the one weakening and dying through sins.

No one has said or written these things against the righteous man; for the Lord would not have rejected him so severely unless he had broken the laws of a state. Furthermore, the drama of the stoning is not less [a target for distortion] (since he also tries to interpret this in a different way), the Gospel text being falsified by saying, 'we have not found very much, having searched in those before this, that the Jews carried stones in order to stone him' (John 10:31); then, after a little, he says: 'if they carried them again, they carried them before.' He wants to construct up and down [arguments] not to precede and another similarly [interpretation], so that he might establish that they carried words, not stones, against him without delay, even though the Evangelist added, having said, 'so they took up stones in order to stone him' (John 10:31). But these things are written in two separate places, and it appears they were done at different times because they do not have the same complexities or pairings of words; but Origen, supposing himself to know all the Scriptures, did not read this, and in writing these things, he treats the whole Gospel as if it were merely a matter of words.
If anyone supposes that we are weaving these things, he will find nothing that we have said to be false by encountering those same Gospel decisions and the studies produced by him regarding this.

But what more is necessary to say? Everything, so to speak, by allegorizing from names, refutes the hypotheses of the facts, not even realizing this: that indeed there are many homonyms of the righteous and the unrighteous, yet it is not possible to judge the dissimilar ways of life from the one same name.

For there is Judas the traitor and another Judas the apostle; or again, Zechariah the most unjust king and another Zechariah the prophet; and not only this, but also Ananias who was thrown into the furnace of fire, and besides this, another Ananias who persecutes the church instead of being persecuted, and instead advocates for the apostle to be beaten, to whom Paul, in a word, responded: 'God is about to beat you, you wall that is plastered (Acts 22:25). And you sit judging me according to the law, and while breaking the law, you command me to be beaten?' Truly, if things are judged by name, let those who...

title: Origen’s allegory; the demon and David’s kingdom
english: Leaning on such allegories, they claim by a mere shared name to interpret unlike sciences or readings of constitutions. Indeed many Jews even today, wrapping themselves in the names of patriarchs or prophets, do unlawful things; and many among the Greeks, called Peter and Paul, do what is ruinous. So Origen’s empty words are caught not least by this kind of light talk. What he brings in wrongly about the resurrection cannot be shown in full here — for Methodius, worthy of holy memory, wrote sufficiently on that theorem and showed plainly that Origen, defining the resurrection on the form rather than on the body itself, unwillingly gave the heretics an opening. That he overturned everything by allegories and sowed seeds of bad doctrine everywhere is easy to see; repeating himself up and down, he filled the inhabited world with unmeasured chatter. By such a method allegorizing everything in every way, he alone could not tropologize the words of the belly-speaker, nor again set out the clear sense from the sequence itself. But what did he bring in besides, inventing escapes by a show of piety? Since the apparition seemed to have said to Saul, “The Lord will tear the kingdom from your hand,” arguing persuasively he answered that one must not think “a demon prophesies about the kingdom of Israel.” Already earlier we said the demon stole these words spoken before by Samuel, so as to deceive the senseless Saul and seem to speak his own. But Origen pretends not to know such dramas of the devil. When it seemed to foretell that the madman’s kingdom would be torn, it then added, “and he will give it to your neighbor, to David.” The much-learned Origen, stirred here, said: “A demon cannot know the kingdom of David appointed by the Lord.” But I am moved to wonder how he carries a reputation for good counsel among the many, as if thoughtful and best in judgment. If the kingdom were unclear, one might somehow feign ignorance under a pretext; but if it was witnessed by God, and Samuel had anointed him for it, and always excelling in the wars he was shown the king’s son-in-law — so that the dancing women ascribed the tens of thousands to him and the thousands to Saul — and if these and such things stood clear, what strange or paradoxical thing was it if the demon recognized the kingdom that exists and was appointed by the Lord through the prophet? For must one not think (if one must say by way of excess that he knows only bodily things) that the anointing with oil has a perceptible application of touch? No one will dispute that these things stand plain to all. And to speak the surplus: even if such things had not stood clear — which would be greater in comparison, to know David’s kingdom, or to bring prophetic souls up from Hades? Yet this too has been shown in the case of the greater person: for even concerning Christ the demons, twisted and unwilling, cry out in so many words, “What have we to do with you, Son of God? Have you come before the time to destroy us?” But to send for souls from Hades and at the same time call down choirs of angels flying from heaven — God alone and his most divine Son have authority to do that; no one else at all. If then they knew God’s invisible kingdom anointed by the Holy Spirit, could they not much more recognize David’s, shown through a perceptible anointing and a visible pouring? Or did the criminal not know what was done and set in the scriptures about David — he who even came to the Lord when he put on the body and said boldly: “If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down; for it is written that he will command his angels concerning you, and they will lift you on their hands, lest you strike your foot against a stone”? So if he is formed to speak from the holy scriptures, he knows what is written — though badly learned; and if he stands in knowledge of these things, he did not fail to know David’s kingdom, which is carved in the sacred letters. Therefore when the demon speaks what is written, he prophesied nothing at all. But the much-famed Origen, finding nothing to say, [turns] to this…

title: The Demon's Limited Power
english: He has naturally fled, and he brings an argument against these things, saying: 'But I,' he says, 'am not able to give such power to a demon, so that he may prophesy concerning Saul and the people of God, and prophesy concerning the kingdoms of David, that he is about to reign.'

Then, someone might say, 'O most foolish of men, you do not grant him to prophesy, yet you permit him to raise up prophets from Hades and to suddenly transfer angelic hosts, which is a greater, more excellent, and more divine thing possessing authority; did anyone then think so weakly or poorly?' But I would most certainly say, having reconsidered, that the demon prophesied nothing, as we also demonstrated further.

If, however, having been judged worthy of prophecy, he did happen to [prophesy], it was not necessary to suppose that the demon raised up spirits and souls from Hades; for even Caiaphas, during the conspiracy against Christ, prophesied, having said: 'It is expedient for us that one man should die for the people, and that the whole nation should not perish' (John 11:50). These things he did not say of himself, just as the most wise John, being a high priest in that year, prophesied.

But here he presents the duality of the Father and the only-begotten Son, one being called the Lord who is being tested, and the other being the beloved Lord and God, in order to show from the duality the one divinity and the true generation of God. If that prophet, promising to show a sign or a wonder, is to answer all things to one who introduces the unlawful idolatry, how much more ought one not to believe a demon promising to transport souls from Hades and spirits of the righteous, even if the power of the sign is working ahead?

But no one would say of the impious that God raised Samuel from the dead to test the unrighteous, desiring that he might write the drama upon the demon's promise and through this appearance deceive some; for it is necessary to guard the holiness of divination from every side, as the Lawgiver established. But is not the cause of augury, the divination of the belly, and the omens of bells considered not secret? Hear how shortly thereafter he again strictly commanded: 'And if you enter the land which the Lord your God gives you, you shall not learn to do according to the abominations of those nations (Deuteronomy 18:10-12). There shall not be found among you one purifying his son or his daughter in the fire, one divining, one using omens, one using bells, one using drugs, one being a medium, and one a wonder-seer, inquiring of the dead. For it is an abomination to the Lord, everyone doing these things.'

After this, warning that he also threatens death and destruction to foreigners because of these things, he immediately added: 'Because of these abominations, the Lord will destroy them from you (Deuteronomy 7:3-4).' It appears, therefore, that the divination of the belly is joined together with all the causes of idolatry, just as if, when scraps lying within are subject to fever, they are accustomed to cause stench and destruction by provoking sickness or burning out the exhausted.

If he also named the deceptive visions as wonder-seeing, as many as are recounted through the belly-diviners, he established that nothing is true in them. From here, I think, he again brought forth a darker decision against them in the Levitical law, bringing words to them: 'And man or woman' saying...
